findings.description: The policy grants full administrative action sets (ec2:*, s3:*, lambda:*, cloudwatch:*) on Resource "*", so a compromised deploy account can read/modify/delete any S3 data, terminate instances, and alter Lambda code and CloudWatch configs across the whole account. It also permits privilege escalation pathways such as iam:PassRole-style abuse via broad service wildcards.

The statement has no Condition block, no explicit Deny, and no permission boundary or resource constraints, so it cannot be narrowed at runtime and applies account-wide. Absence of scoping conditions (e.g. aws:RequestedRegion, MFA) means any use of the credentials yields unrestricted API access.

A static IAM access key is created for the svc_deploy user instead of using short-lived credentials (OIDC federation or IAM Roles Anywhere). These keys never expire, can be silently exfiltrated, and are not tied to a specific workload identity.

findings.issue_category: secret key material exposed in state
findings.description: The secret access key is generated by this resource and is by design stored in plaintext in Terraform state and passed through outputs. Combined with the write-only nature of access keys this exposes the credential to anyone with access to the state backend or the output value.

The output exposes secret key material without the sensitive = true flag, so the value is printed in plan/apply logs and CI console output and is not redacted in downstream use. Anyone with read access to the Terraform output or logs obtains the credential.

The IAM user holding broad deployment permissions has no MFA device requirement or associated policy enforcing MFA, so possession of the static access key alone is sufficient to authenticate and act with administrative scope.
